reference.source: Volpe's Neurology of the Newborn / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy that, like Walker-Warburg syndrome, combines brain malformation, eye anomalies, and muscular dystrophy, but is generally less severe
It was classically described in the Finnish population and is often linked to variants in POMGNT1, though other glycosylation genes can cause an overlapping phenotype
Brain imaging shows a cobblestone-type cortical malformation, typically with frontoparietal predominance, cerebellar hypoplasia or cysts, brainstem hypoplasia, and often hydrocephalus and flat pons
Ocular features include severe myopia, glaucoma, retinal dysplasia, and progressive visual impairment
Affected children have congenital hypotonia and weakness with raised serum creatine kinase, and many achieve some developmental milestones unlike the more severe Walker-Warburg phenotype
It sits on a clinical continuum between Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy and Walker-Warburg syndrome within the dystroglycanopathies
Diagnosis combines the MRI pattern, ophthalmological findings, elevated creatine kinase, and molecular testing
reference.pathophysiology: Muscle-eye-brain disease is a dystroglycanopathy caused by biallelic variants in genes required for O-glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan, classically POMGNT1. Deficient glycosylation impairs the binding of alpha-dystroglycan to extracellular matrix components, weakening basement membranes in brain, eye, and muscle. Disruption of the pial limiting membrane during corticogenesis permits neuronal over-migration and cobblestone cortical malformation, while the same molecular defect produces retinal and anterior segment anomalies and a congenital muscular dystrophy. The phenotype is intermediate in severity within the dystroglycanopathy spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Walker-Warburg syndrome at the severe end of the spectrum
Other congenital muscular dystrophies with eye involvement
Congenital glaucoma or high myopia of other cause
Congenital infection with brain and eye malformation
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI for cobblestone cortex, cerebellar and brainstem anomalies, and hydrocephalus
Ophthalmological assessment for myopia, glaucoma, and retinal dysplasia
Molecular genetic testing including POMGNT1 and a dystroglycanopathy panel
Muscle biopsy with alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation studies if needed
Developmental assessment and electroencephalography where seizures occur
redFlags: Raised intraocular pressure from glaucoma threatening vision
Respiratory or feeding compromise from muscle weakness
reference.prognosis: Muscle-eye-brain disease is generally less severe than Walker-Warburg syndrome, and many children survive into later childhood or adulthood with variable intellectual disability, motor impairment, epilepsy, and progressive visual loss. Prognosis depends on the severity of the brain malformation and systemic complications.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish it from Walker-Warburg syndrome, leading to inaccurate prognostic counselling
Overlooking treatable ocular complications such as glaucoma
Not recognising the muscular dystrophy component and its raised creatine kinase
Assuming a specific gene when the dystroglycanopathies show considerable phenotypic overlap
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; management is supportive and multidisciplinary across the neuromuscular, brain and eye involvement
Neurological care with antiepileptic drugs for seizures and neurosurgical CSF diversion (ventriculoperitoneal shunt) for hydrocephalus
Ophthalmic management of severe myopia, glaucoma and retinal dysplasia, with refractive correction and glaucoma treatment to preserve vision
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and orthopaedic care for hypotonia, weakness and contractures from the congenital muscular dystrophy
Nutritional and respiratory support, with feeding and airway assessment as weakness progresses
Developmental support and monitoring, with electroencephalography where seizures occur
Autosomal recessive dystroglycanopathy (POMGNT1) genetic counselling and family testing
